body.heading: The old answer that does not quite work
paragraphs: For over a century, the standard explanation was pressure melting: ice is unusual in that squeezing it lowers its melting point, so the pressure under a skate blade or a boot was said to melt a thin film of water that lubricates the slide. The physics is real — but the numbers are too small. At temperatures well below freezing, no reasonable pressure melts enough ice to explain how slippery it stays.

The giveaway is that ice is slippery even to something just standing on it, barely pressing at all, and remains slippery at −20 °C, where pressure melting is hopeless. Something about the surface of ice itself had to be doing the work.

body.heading: The modern answer: a surface that is never quite solid
paragraphs: Michael Faraday suspected the truth in the 1850s: the outermost layer of ice is disordered and liquid-like even below freezing. Modern instruments have confirmed it. Molecules at the surface have neighbours missing on one side, so they are loosely bound and mobile, forming a film only nanometres thick that behaves partly like water.

When you slide, friction adds its own contribution, melting a little more water as you go — the two effects together make ice's lubricating layer. That is why a fast skate glides so freely, and why the slipperiness fades in extreme cold, around −30 °C and below, where the liquid-like layer thins and stiffens.

body.heading: Living with a slippery surface
paragraphs: Understanding the film explains the countermeasures. Sand and grit do not melt anything; they give shoes something solid to bite into, breaking through the film to the rough ice beneath. Winter tyres use soft rubber and fine cuts in the tread to grip a surface that defeats ordinary tyres.

It also explains a small mystery of the rink: ice is at its slipperiest near melting point, not in deep cold. Skaters in a refrigerated arena are gliding, quite literally, on a skin of water that the ice can never quite freeze shut.

description: Pressure melting alone cannot explain slippery ice. The honest modern answer is a nanometre-thin liquid-like layer on ice's surface.
